A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Collaborative Gym framework, agents, and task environments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated benchmarks, a study involving 99 participants and 150 collaboration trajectories, and annotated error analyses (Tables 2–4).

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds a real-user interaction ablation, simulator validation, and step-limit analyses (Table 6, Appendix D, and Table 8).

M1.justification: The CoEnv interface, collaboration actions, notification algorithm, ReAct agents, Scratchpad, and situational-planning procedure remain unchanged, including the appendix prompts and pseudocode. The turn-taking variant is an experimental ablation, not a replacement for the proposed framework.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Travel Planning using TravelPlanner, Related Work using arXiv CS papers, and Tabular Analysis using DiscoveryBench, under simulated and real conditions. The new analyses retain this task coverage; the turn-taking ablation changes interaction procedures. Mentioned computer-use environments have no reported evaluation.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain the same three agent types and four underlying LMs. v3 adds Turn-taking Co-Gym as an evaluated comparator in Table 6. CowPilot and other frameworks in the new related-work table are descriptive comparisons, not additional experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v3 removes Collaboration Score and Controlled Autonomy metrics from the evaluation suite. It adds a matched real-user ablation with 20 cases per task, always running turn-taking before non-turn-taking (Appendix F.3), plus simulator quality and distinguishability annotation protocols. The original benchmark subsets, model configurations, temperature, and 30-step limit are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted tests of the notification protocol, simulator accuracy/consistency/plausibility, and whether annotators can distinguish simulated from real trajectories. Table 8 additionally examines how often agents exhaust the step budget, and Section 5.2 quantifies alignment between existing error distributions. The original detailed error taxonomy and illustrated case studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Table 4 adds 95% confidence intervals to the retained human win rates. New analyses report a binomial test for simulator distinguishability and significance for the error-distribution correlation. The original benchmark t-tests and McNemar tests remain; neither version documents an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Comparable main benchmark values and human win rates remain unchanged. New results include 70% preference for non-turn-taking in both ablation tasks, simulator ratings of 93.0% accuracy, 92.0% consistency, and 90.3% plausibility, and step-limit frequencies. Collaboration Score and Controlled Autonomy results are removed. v3 also introduces an inconsistent abstract figure: 80% real-world situational-awareness failures versus the retained 40% in Tables 5 and 10.

T1.justification: v1's mathematical definition of Collaboration Score as the delivery indicator multiplied by Task Performance is removed. The POMDP formulation and Initiative Entropy definition remain equivalent. Neither version contains substantive theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central framework and collaboration-benefit claims persist. v3 qualifies its novelty around dual control and non-turn-taking interaction, explicitly claims a reliable user simulator and publicly released infrastructure, and narrows the abstract's performance statement to the best-performing collaborative agents. Collaboration Score and Controlled Autonomy are no longer presented as contributions.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new studies as supporting simulator realism and more flexible, teammate-like interaction. It removes v1's detailed discussion of particular failures being more prevalent with real users and of cross-session personalization limitations. The basic limitations concerning three-task coverage and a restricted participant population remain in Appendix A.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code/data release, whereas v3 reports public MIT-licensed availability of the framework, environments, agents, and evaluation scripts, a substantial change in documented reproducibility access. v3 also supplies hosting hardware specifications, judge temperature, and implementation details for the new ablation. These are reported disclosures; repository availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially replaces the discussion of Markov games, PettingZoo, and broader robotics/HCI collaboration with positioning around single versus dual control and turn-taking versus non-turn-taking. It adds explicit comparisons with CowPilot, tau-Bench, and tau2-Bench, alongside expanded agent-evaluation and simulator references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Conditions and tasks change order, the separate in-depth-analysis section is integrated into experiments, and appendices are reorganized with a contents page. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, and Figure 1's stacked panels become side-by-side. Benchmark tables are restructured, new comparison and analysis tables appear, and the detailed error table moves to the appendix with a summary table in the main text. Controlled Autonomy prompt figures disappear, while retained prompts and trajectory figures are redistributed.

improvement.justification: The notification ablation and simulator validation provide useful evidence for central framework choices that v1 supported mainly through rationale and benchmark observations; confidence intervals also improve reporting. The gains are limited by the ablation's fixed condition order, loss of Controlled Autonomy evidence, and v3's new abstract error reporting 80% real-world situational-awareness failures despite unchanged tables showing 40%. Overall, the empirical support improves modestly rather than decisively.
